subtitle: The common rotating interface
description: A 400 mm disc and detachable flanged hub define a shared prototype interface. The drum variant appears in the drum-brake package. This is a geometry study, not a speed-rated rotor.
targets: Shaft, balance and thermal assessment required
decisions: Use a detachable hub to replace the friction disc without replacing the shaft interface.
Begin with machined steel for prototype traceability; evaluate a cast-iron friction variant only through paired friction and thermal tests.
Use one six-hole interface across the first disc concepts; bolt preload and joint slip capacity remain to be sized.
materials: Disc: C45 normalized steel candidate; friction compound must be qualified with this surface.
Hub: 42CrMo4 quenched-and-tempered candidate; property certificate must correspond to actual section size.
risks: Disc-to-hub torque transfer, bolt preload and fatigue are not yet established.
No keyway or locking element is released; the 50 mm bore is an interface placeholder.
Thermal coning, hot runout, balance and overspeed remain unverified.
steps: Inspect disc and hub identification, bore and interface faces.
Locate disc on the hub spigot; align six through holes.
Fit the specified through-bolts, washers and nuts after joint design is approved.
Measure assembled runout and balance before guarded testing.
validation: Thermal transient model with moving pad heat flux and measured heat partition.
Bolted joint slip, bearing, hub torsion and rotational stress calculations.
Guarded speed, runout, balance and repeated stop tests.
hypotheses: Time disc replacement versus a documented integral-hub baseline with the same shaft access.
Count unique components across the disc-brake concepts; this is not a competitor advantage claim.
sensors: Reserve non-contact runout measurement access and a temperature observation window.

subtitle: The first service-brake platform
description: A spring-applied, thruster-released 315 mm drum concept with replaceable shoes, accessible pivots and a fabricated base. DIN compatibility is a future interface check, not claimed by this geometry.
decisions: Buy a qualified thruster first; put development effort into accessible metalwork and service interfaces.
Keep pivot pins and bushes separately replaceable rather than boring directly into welded levers.
Use a fabricated prototype base; casting economics follow actual batch volumes.
materials: Base and lever plate: S355J2+N candidate; weld procedure and fatigue detail approval required.
Pins: 42CrMo4 candidate with controlled finish; bushes: purchased bearing-grade bronze candidate.
Lining: bought, characterized non-asbestos compound; bonding and mechanical retention require supplier approval.
risks: Equalization, spring linkage and actuator transmission are layout placeholders; motion is not solved.
The assumed torque is not a rating and does not cover an emergency stop or hoist safety case.
Shoe contact geometry, drum heating and pivot loads require coupled assessment.
steps: Locate base on the test fixture and inspect pivot-centre coordinates.
Fit clevis supports, levers, bushes and retained pivot pins.
Install carriers and lining; centre the drum and establish cold clearance.
Install purchased thruster and engineered equalizing/spring linkage after kinematic approval.
Check full release motion without friction contact before load testing.
validation: Kinematic travel/clearance and load transfer before structural FEA.
Lever/pin bearing, bending, base weld fatigue and drum thermal calculations.
Static holding, dynamic torque, application/release time and endurance tests with the chosen lining.
hypotheses: Timed same-duty shoe replacement against a selected conventional assembly.
Compare two quotes for plate fabrication with equivalent cast components.
sensors: Advisory position / wear sensing with replaceable brackets; no AI-controlled brake release.
Record supplier sensor range, supply, connector, EMC, ingress and temperature limits before selection.
Define independent machine safety interface and diagnostic fault response with the responsible controls engineer.

sensors: Advisory position / wear sensing with replaceable brackets; no AI-controlled brake release.

subtitle: An absorber integration, not a brake
description: A replaceable purchased energy absorber, bumper face and bolted mounting plate for a later crane end-stop programme. Absorber internals and force-stroke characteristics are not designed.
targets: E / s only; peak force unknown
Impact mass, speed and duty required
decisions: Partner with an absorber specialist rather than infer impact qualification from brake work.
Use a replaceable mounting interface and visible stroke envelope.
Size the machine attachment for verified peak force, not E/s average.
materials: Mounting plate: S355J2+N candidate.
Absorber and bumper face: supplier-controlled hydraulic/elastomer components.
risks: No metering geometry, damping curve or peak force established.
Travel envelope does not demonstrate energy absorption.
steps: Collect impact mass, speed, available stroke and recovery interval.
Select rated absorber and replace CAD envelope with supplier model.
Approve foundation fasteners and collision clearance.
validation: Supplier force-stroke curve and machine structure analysis.
Instrumented impact, temperature and repeated-impact tests.
hypotheses: Compare removable cartridge service with the customer baseline.
No performance multiple assigned before impact testing.
sensors: Stroke/end-position and impact-event recording only; define survival environment and cable protection.

subtitle: A separate storm-holding programme
description: A rail-head clamp packaging study with opposed shoes and an actuator envelope. Rail dimensions, wedge/spring mechanism and certified holding force require an application-specific design.
decisions: Require the actual rail profile and wind-load analysis before developing a clamp mechanism.
Partner with a specialist for first installations.
Keep contamination and rail surface variation central to the requirements.
materials: Frame: S355J2+N candidate only; loads may force a different section or material.
Rail shoes: supplier friction system; rail damage compatibility must be assessed.
risks: No functional wedge, latch or spring mechanism is modelled.
High required normal forces make this an application-specific structural programme.
No personnel-transport, storm safety or hazardous-area approval.
steps: Obtain rail profile, rail restraint, wind loads and failure-state requirements.
Approve specialist mechanism and dimensional interface.
Finalize clamps, foundation, guarding and independent verification.
validation: Wind load and machine/rail load path analysis.
Wet/oily rail holding tests, release clearance and fault testing.
hypotheses: Compare only tested units on the same rail, contamination and load case.
sensors: Advisory position / wear sensing with replaceable brackets; no AI-controlled brake release.
Record supplier sensor range, supply, connector, EMC, ingress and temperature limits before selection.
